meta.title: Polish elections
sources: Wikipedia: Polish parliamentary and presidential election articles, 1919–2025, and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth's royal free elections, 1573–1764 (results, infoboxes and leads)

presEras.label: The Commonwealth's royal elections
presEras.blurb: For two centuries the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth elected its kings: every nobleman had the right to ride to the election field at Wola and vote, a franchise of hundreds of thousands when western Europe's parliaments answered to dozens. Eleven free elections chose monarchs from Valois to Poniatowski — until the neighbouring powers learned to buy the outcome.

presEras.label: The Second Republic and after
presEras.blurb: Reborn Poland's presidents were chosen by the National Assembly: the 1922 election ended with Gabriel Narutowicz assassinated within a week; the 1926 vote followed Piłsudski's coup — he declined the office he had just won — and 1947's was the communist takeover ratifying itself.

presEras.label: The direct-election era
presEras.blurb: The 1989 round-table parliament narrowly elected Jaruzelski; from 1990 Poland has chosen its president by direct two-round vote — Wałęsa's rise and fall, the Kaczyński era and the Smolensk shadow over 2010, and the knife-edge runoffs of 2020 and 2025.

legEras.label: The Second Republic
legEras.blurb: The reborn state's Sejm began with the 1919 constituent election and grew fractious fast. After Piłsudski's 1926 coup the sanacja regime bent the process — the 1930 'Brest election' jailed opposition leaders, and the opposition boycotted 1935 and 1938.

legEras.label: The People's Republic
legEras.blurb: The 1947 election was rigged outright; from 1952 voters were handed a single Front of National Unity list. Recorded here as rituals of the communist state, not elections — until the system cracked.

legEras.label: The round-table breakthrough
legEras.blurb: The June 1989 election was semi-free by design: the opposition could contest all Senate seats and a third of the Sejm. Solidarity won everything it was allowed to contest, the arrangement collapsed under the result, and communist rule in Poland ended within months.

legEras.label: The Third Republic
legEras.blurb: Fully free elections from 1991: hyper-fragmentation, consolidation into the Civic Platform–Law and Justice duopoly, PiS's 2015 and 2019 majorities, and the record-turnout 2023 election that changed the government again.

presAfter.name: Henri de Valois
presAfter.party: The free election of 1573 was the first ever royal election to be held in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. It attracted an estimated 40,000–50,000 szlachta (Polish nobility) voters (the highest turnout ever) who elected Henry of Valois king.

presidential.summary: The free election was introduced due to the childless death of the last Jagiellonian monarch Sigismund II Augustus and the lack of a potential candidate that would satisfy most of the nobles.
presidential.caveat: A royal free election of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth: the assembled nobility chose the king. Vast for its era, the franchise was still nobility-only — and later elections were swayed openly by foreign money and armies.

presidential.summary: The free election of 1576 was the second royal election to be held in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which took place in 1575/1576. In the night of June 28–29, 1574, King Henry III of France secretly left Poland to claim the French throne.
presidential.caveat: A royal free election of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth: the assembled nobility chose the king. Vast for its era, the franchise was still nobility-only — and later elections were swayed openly by foreign money and armies.

presAfter.name: Sigismund III Vasa
presAfter.party: The free election of 1587 was the third royal election to be held in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which took place after the death of King Stefan Batory. It began on June 30, 1587, when Election Sejm was summoned in the village of Wola near Warsaw, and ended on December 27 of the same year, when King Sigismund III was crowned in Kraków’s Wawel Cathedral.

presAfter.name: Władysław IV Vasa
presAfter.party: The 1632 free election in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth commenced between September 27 and November 8, 1632. It then extended to November 13, 1632. The election sejm elevated Władysław IV to the Polish throne. Władysław had won the support of most of the political factions; and in the absence of any other serious contenders, he was elected King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania.

presAfter.name: John II Casimir Vasa
presAfter.party: The 1648 free election in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth began on 6 October 1648, and ended on November 17 of the same year. The new King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania was John II Casimir, the younger brother of previous king, Władysław IV, who had died on May 20, 1648.

presidential.summary: On 16 September 1668, King John II Casimir abdicated the Polish–Lithuanian throne. He left for France and joined the Jesuits where he became Abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés Abbey in Paris which resulted in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth being left without a monarch, making an election necessary.
presidential.caveat: A royal free election of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth: the assembled nobility chose the king. Vast for its era, the franchise was still nobility-only — and later elections were swayed openly by foreign money and armies.

presidential.summary: On November 10, 1673, Michael Korybut Wiśniowiecki, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania, suddenly died in Lwów. The Polish throne was vacant again, so another free election was necessary.
presidential.caveat: A royal free election of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth: the assembled nobility chose the king. Vast for its era, the franchise was still nobility-only — and later elections were swayed openly by foreign money and armies.

presidential.summary: One of the candidates for the Polish throne was the Duke of Oława (Lower Silesia) and son of the late king, James Louis Sobieski. He was initially supported by the Kingdom of France and the Swedish Empire.
presidential.caveat: A royal free election of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth: the assembled nobility chose the king. Vast for its era, the franchise was still nobility-only — and later elections were swayed openly by foreign money and armies.

presidential.summary: In early 1700, King of Poland, Grand Duke of Lithuania and Elector of Saxony, Augustus II the Strong began the Great Northern War by attacking Swedish Livonia. Despite Russian support, Saxon army lost several battles, and soon afterwards, forces of the Swedish Empire controlled most of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.

presidential.summary: On February 1, 1733, the King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania Augustus II the Strong died in Warsaw, leaving the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth without a monarch. Another royal election was necessary.
presidential.caveat: A royal free election of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth: the assembled nobility chose the king. Vast for its era, the franchise was still nobility-only — and later elections were swayed openly by foreign money and armies.

presidential.summary: The Seven Years' War, which ended in 1763, established a new pattern of political alliances in Europe. The Kingdom of Prussia, the Kingdom of Great Britain and the Russian Empire emerged as great powers, while the position of Austria, France, Spain, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire was weakened.
presidential.caveat: A royal free election of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth: the assembled nobility chose the king. Vast for its era, the franchise was still nobility-only — and later elections were swayed openly by foreign money and armies.

presidential.summary: Two indirect presidential elections were held in Poland in December 1922. In the first election on 9 December Gabriel Narutowicz was elected president, but he was assassinated five days later.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote of the National Assembly, not a popular election.

presidential.summary: There were two candidates: Piłsudski and supported by the National Democracy, Christian Democracy and Piast Adolf Bniński, Voivode of Poznań.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote of the National Assembly, not a popular election.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Poland on May 8, 1933. Professor Ignacy Mościcki was re-elected for a second seven-year term, having previously been elected to the position in 1926.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote of the National Assembly, not a popular election.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Poland on February 5th 1947, the last presidential elections until 1989. The president had to be elected by the newly formed Legislative Sejm among presented candidates.
presidential.caveat: Held by a legislature produced by a rigged election, under communist control.

presidential.summary: Indirect presidential elections were held in Poland on 19 July 1989. The elections were the first after the office of President of the Republic of Poland had been re-established after a period of Communist rule and were the last in which the President was elected by Parliament (joint houses of the Sejm and Senate).
presidential.caveat: Elected by the round-table parliament, not by popular vote — by a single vote's margin.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Poland on 25 November 1990, with a second round on 9 December. They were the first direct presidential elections in the history of Poland, and the first free presidential elections since the May Coup of 1926.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Poland on 5 November 1995, with a second round on 19 November. The leader of Social Democracy, Aleksander Kwaśniewski, and incumbent President Lech Wałęsa advanced to the second round.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Poland on 8 October 2000. Incumbent President Aleksander Kwaśniewski was easily re-elected in the first round with more than 50% of the vote, the only time a direct presidential election in Poland has not gone to a second round.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Poland on 9 October and 23 October 2005. The outgoing President of Poland, Aleksander Kwaśniewski, had served the two five-year terms allowed under the constitution and was unable to stand for a third term.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Poland on 20 June 2010. As no candidate received a majority of votes in the first round, a second round was held on 4 July 2010.
Presidential elections were held in Poland on 10 and 24 May 2015.

Presidential elections were held in Poland on 28 June 2020. As no candidate received a majority of the vote, a second round was held on 12 July, in which incumbent president Andrzej Duda, running with the support of the incumbent government of the Law and Justice (PiS) party, faced off against Civic Platform vice-chairman and Mayor of Warsaw Rafał Trzaskowski.
Presidential elections were held in Poland on 18 May 2025. As no candidate received a majority of the vote, a second round was held on 1 June 2025.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 26 January 1919, electing the first Sejm of the Second Polish Republic. The elections, based on universal suffrage and proportional representation, was the first free election in the country's history.

parties.name: Union of Jewish National Parties in Lesser Poland

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 5 November 1922, with Senate elections held a week later on 12 November. The elections were governed by the March Constitution of Poland, and saw the Christian Union of National Unity coalition emerge as the largest bloc in the Sejm with 163 of the 444 seats.

parties.name: Nonpartisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 4 March 1928, with Senate elections held a week later on 11 March. The Nonpartisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government, a coalition of the Sanation faction - won the highest number of seats in the Sejm (125 out of 444) and 48 out of 111 in the Senate–in both cases, short of a majority.

parties.name: Nonpartisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 16 November 1930, with Senate elections held a week later on 23 November. In what became known as the Brest elections (Polish: Wybory brzeskie), the pro-Sanation Nonpartisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government took 47% of the vote and 249 of the 444 seats in Sejm and 77 of the 111 seats in the Senate.
legislative.caveat: Held with opposition leaders imprisoned in the Brest fortress and the state apparatus mobilised for the government list.

parties.name: Nonpartisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 8 September 1935, with Senate elections held a week later on 15 September. They were held under the April Constitution, drawn up earlier in 1935 by the Sanation movement, which had changed the electoral system to one more in its favor.
legislative.caveat: Held under the sanacja regime's 1935 constitution and boycotted by the main opposition parties.
legislative.seatLeader: Nonpartisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 6 November 1938, with Senate elections held a week later on 13 November. They were the last elections in the Second Polish Republic.
legislative.caveat: Held under the sanacja regime's 1935 constitution and boycotted by the main opposition parties.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 19 January 1947, the first since World War II.
legislative.caveat: Rigged outright: the count was falsified and the opposition terrorised. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 26 October 1952. They were the first elections to the Sejm, the parliament of the Polish People's Republic.
legislative.caveat: A single-list vote of the communist People's Republic, with no opposition permitted. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 20 January 1957. They were the second election to the Sejm – the unicameral parliament of the People's Republic of Poland, and the third ever in the history of Communist Poland.
legislative.caveat: A single-list vote of the communist People's Republic, with no opposition permitted. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: The 1961 elections followed the liberalized rules prepared for those in 1957, but compared to the situation five years ago, the Polish society was much more apathetic and disappointed with the government.
legislative.caveat: A single-list vote of the communist People's Republic, with no opposition permitted. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 30 May 1965. They were the fourth elections to the Sejm of the People's Republic of Poland, and fifth in Communist Poland.
legislative.caveat: A single-list vote of the communist People's Republic, with no opposition permitted. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 1 June 1969. The results, like with the other elections in communist Poland, were controlled by the communist government.
legislative.caveat: A single-list vote of the communist People's Republic, with no opposition permitted. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 4 June 1989 to elect members of the Sejm and the recreated Senate, with a second round on 18 June.
legislative.caveat: Semi-free by agreement: the opposition could contest all Senate seats but only a third of the Sejm. Within those limits, Solidarity swept everything.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 27 October 1991 to elect deputies to the First Term Sejm and the Senate, the two houses of the National Assembly. The 1991 election was notable on several counts.

Parliamentary elections were held in Poland on 13 October 2019. All 460 members of the Sejm and 100 senators of the Senate were elected.

In the previous 2019 Polish parliamentary election, the ruling right-wing Law and Justice Party (PiS) had held onto its majority in the Sejm with Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki forming a second government. The PiS sought to win a third term which would be unprecedented in Polish history.
